entries.name: Stochastic Expectation Maximization
entries.definition: A finite-mixture fitting algorithm that draws one hard component assignment for each observation from its current posterior responsibilities, fits the resulting completed-data model, and recomputes the responsibilities for the next iteration.
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes the Celeux-Diebolt stochastic-completion construction. It is a single-completion specialization of Monte Carlo EM and corresponds algebraically to a one-draw, unit-weight replacement in the SAEM recursion, rather than decreasing-step recursive averaging. Its named stochastic process and stationary-summary interpretation differ from CEM posterior-mode assignment, supplemented-EM covariance estimation, general ICE estimator averaging and Bayesian sampling of model parameters. Bare SEM is not asserted as a unique alias. No normalized identity matches among 442 pinned and 473 maintained records, including the bare acronym probes. Existing supplemented EM and cross-entropy optimization are distinct methods; qualified aliases avoid claiming SEM or CEM as unique names. ICE, MCEM, SAEM, deterministic tempered EM, simulated annealing and k-means provide neighboring but different scopes. Existing stochastic-EM frontier and incidental references are not records of the new identities. The absence assessment is bounded to this snapshot and corpus. aio_mappings.rationale: The procedure estimates finite-mixture parameters from observed unlabeled data. The AIO target denotes a learning task/process; this algorithm-to-task relation is not equivalence or a subclass assertion.

claims.statement: For current weights and component densities, normalize p_k f_k(x_i) over k to obtain responsibilities t_ik. Independently draw a categorical label for each observation under t_i, then maximize the completed-data log likelihood. With unrestricted mixture weights the update is the sampled class count divided by N; each component parameter uses its assigned observations and the selected distribution family. Recompute responsibilities from the fit. The original cyclic S-M-E presentation is equivalent to E-S-M when starting from current parameters.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, pp.40-41 / PDF7-8

claims.statement: Random complete-data refitting can retain fluctuations on a fixed observed data set. The source proposes summary means and variances after a stationary regime, rather than equating every iterate with a converged point estimate. Its stated asymptotic result is restricted to two components with an unknown mixing proportion and refers to an earlier technical proof; the general extension is conjectural. A reliable universal burn-in cutoff, unbiased estimator or global maximum is not established.

evidence.locator: Sections 4.2-4.4, pp.41-42 / PDF8-9

claims.statement: The stated baseline restarts when a sampled class has fewer than N*c(N,d) observations. A later practical variant instead deletes a class with count at most d and continues with one fewer component. Restart and deletion define different transition and model-order behavior. Neither automatic component-count recovery nor ergodicity follows from the unprotected assignment/count formula: a zero weight can make that component unreachable.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1, p.40 / PDF7; Section 4.3, p.42 / PDF9; Section 5.4, p.49 / PDF16

claims.statement: A sampled hard partition is not the actual posterior-responsibility matrix. The entropy identity for the actual posterior does not imply equality of completed and marginal likelihood for arbitrary sampled labels, contrary to the report prose following Eq4.4. The saved normalized Bernoulli-mixture example has a positive-probability nonempty completion whose fitted mixing weight decreases marginal likelihood. Per-step ordinary EM ascent therefore cannot be inherited by this stochastic update.

evidence.locator: Section 4.1 Eq4.2-4.4 and following prose, p.9 / PDF11; curator finite-mixture counterexample

limitations: Source stationarity claims depend on the complete transition construction, admissible fits and recurrence assumptions. The original 1985 English article, 1984 proof report and distinct 1986 INRIA RR563 were not fully inspected; generic stationary normality, point convergence or global convergence is not certified.

Model-specific completed-data estimators matter. Empty or undersized classes, unbounded Gaussian fits and identifiability up to label permutation require explicit treatment. The raw formula alone does not specify those policies.

The 1986 numerical tables use 1000 post-stationary iterations, not 1000 independent data sets; their mean-plus/minus-SD summaries are not calibrated confidence intervals. Printed component-weight, mean-sign and component-location discrepancies remain unresolved, so no quantitative superiority or recovery claim is curated.

The optional posterior-threshold classification can leave points unassigned; at threshold one half, tied probabilities can place a point in more than one set. It is a separate readout from the stochastic fitting transition.
No author implementation or historical numerical experiment was reproduced. Finite curator calculations check formula boundaries, not empirical performance or a repaired convergence proof.

claims.statement: Compute t_ik proportional to p_k f_k(x_i) at the current fit. Assign observation i to a maximizing component; the inspected report chooses the smallest component index on ties. Fit parameters by maximizing the hard-assignment completed log likelihood. When mixing weights are estimated, p_k becomes n_k/N and each component fit uses its assigned data. Exact admissible C and M steps make that classification criterion nondecreasing; undefined or singular maximizers need an explicit policy.

evidence.locator: Section 3 Eq3.1-3.4, p.5 / PDF7; Proposition 2, pp.6-7 / PDF8-9

claims.statement: The mixture classification criterion is sum_i log[p_(z_i) f_(z_i)(x_i)], which includes sum_k n_k log p_k. The separate-sampling criterion omits that weight term. With fixed equal weights and a common spherical Gaussian covariance, assignment to the nearest mean and centroid refitting recover the k-means variance objective. Estimating arbitrary mixing weights or using unequal covariances changes the assignment geometry and objective.

evidence.locator: Section 2 Eq2.3-2.7 and Proposition 1, pp.3-4 / PDF5-6; Section 3, p.5 / PDF7

claims.statement: Classification-likelihood ascent is not marginal-mixture likelihood ascent: the saved two-component Bernoulli example increases the former and decreases the latter in one nonempty CEM step. The report’s general claim that CEM classes have disjoint convex hulls also fails for unequal-variance Gaussian components; the saved one-dimensional example assigns outer points to a broad component and inner points to a narrow one. Those limitations do not negate the restricted equal-covariance k-means case.

evidence.locator: Proposition 2, pp.6-7 / PDF8-9; Section 4.1 convex-hull prose, p.10 / PDF12; curator finite counterexamples

claims.statement: The finite-partition argument for stabilization needs admissible finite profiled objectives and well-defined maximizer selection; it is not a global-optimum guarantee. Initial partitions and ties can affect the solution. The local-rate proposition invokes stronger curvature and coordinate-optimization assumptions. Because the relaxed objective is affine in the assignment matrix, no generic negative-definite assignment Hessian or universal linear-rate claim is certified here.

evidence.locator: Propositions 2-3 and following discussion, pp.6-8 / PDF8-10; Eq2.3-2.5, pp.3-4 / PDF5-6

limitations: The inspected primary version is the January 1991 author report, not the inaccessible 1992 journal full text. Eq2.2 prints a malformed marginal likelihood without the component sum; the mixture law in Eq2.1 determines the correct normalization. Eq2.7 doubles the variable-dependent Gaussian log-likelihood terms, leaving the displayed optimizer but not literal likelihood values unchanged.

Hard reassignment can empty a component; unrestricted component likelihoods can become singular or unbounded. Fixed component count, nonempty partitions and finite M-step solutions are not guaranteed by an argmax assignment alone.

The source’s local-rate proof and its external grouped-coordinate theorem were not independently repaired. Affine assignment dependence and boundary solutions require care before importing smooth interior curvature claims.

The numerical experiments evaluate a variance criterion under selected mixture and serum-data settings. A practical SEM-then-CEM hybrid is distinct from pure CEM; no universal superiority, generalization or semantic-cluster claim is curated.
No author implementation or historical numerical experiment was reproduced. Finite curator calculations check formula boundaries, not empirical performance or a repaired convergence proof.

entries.name: Classification Annealing Expectation Maximization
entries.definition: A stochastic hard-clustering algorithm that samples component assignments from current mixture posterior probabilities raised to an inverse positive temperature, maximizes the completed-data classification likelihood, and lowers the temperature according to a chosen schedule.
entries.identity_notes: The Celeux-Govaert CAEM construction changes the random label distribution within classification EM. It differs from deterministic tempered EM, decreasing-step sufficient-statistic SAEM, and Metropolis simulated annealing with an accept/reject transition. Temperature one recovers the SEM assignment law; the low-temperature limit concentrates on maximal posterior components but retains random choice among ties. claims.statement: At temperature tau_m>0, set s_ik proportional to [p_k f_k(x_i)]^(1/tau_m), equivalently t_ik^(1/tau_m), and normalize across components. Draw a hard label independently for each observation from s_i and maximize the corresponding completed-data likelihood. The power applies to the entire weight-times-density product. The next iteration uses the updated parameters and scheduled temperature; it is not a fractional-responsibility M-step or a Metropolis acceptance test.

evidence.locator: Section 4.2 Eq4.6, p.11 / PDF13; Section 3 M-step, p.5 / PDF7

claims.statement: At tau=1, the assignment law equals SEM. Holding positive component scores fixed while tau approaches zero concentrates mass on maximal scores; with multiple tied maxima, their limiting probabilities are equal rather than the smallest-index tie choice specified for deterministic CEM. Literal division by tau=0 is undefined. This fixed-score limit does not establish that a changing-parameter cooling run converges to a global solution.

evidence.locator: Section 4.2 Eq4.6 and SEM/CEM interpolation discussion, p.11 / PDF13; Section 3 tie rule, p.5 / PDF7; curator temperature and tie calculations

claims.statement: The report gives geometric cooling tau_(m+1)=a*tau_m as a practical choice and explicitly says its analogous CAEM convergence result has not yet been proved. The printed range includes a=1, which does not cool. Its experiments use a=0.97 and stop when a partition is unchanged; an unchanged stochastic partition over a finite comparison is not proof of future absorption. Neither a geometric schedule nor the simulated-annealing analogy supplies a global-convergence guarantee.

evidence.locator: Section 4.2 cooling and convergence discussion, p.12 / PDF14; Section 5 experimental settings, pp.12-13 / PDF14-15

native_neighbors.identity_notes: ICE specifies expectation of an estimator, not maximization of an expected complete-data log likelihood as in EM. The estimator may be maximum likelihood, least squares or another supported complete-data estimator. Shared applications to hidden Markov models do not make ICE a model family, an ICM label optimizer or a synonym for every stochastic EM method. Its behavior depends on the selected estimator and parameterization. The short acronym is scoped to this estimation procedure. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels and all scoped synonyms and 394 preceding native IDs, names and aliases for these three concepts. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, yielding 64 and 64 matched lines; all 44 unique contents were read. Hits represent neighboring records, citations and discovery leads rather than records of these identities. All 97 semantic label/synonym hits were read. Twenty-one fully annotated exact CLASS nodes and outgoing edges were verified identical to the preceding inspection, and three additional nodes were read. Twenty-eight contextual YAMLs were byte-verified after prior full reading and four freshly read, totaling 24 generated and eight native contextual records. Short acronyms were included in the complete normalized identity comparison. The absence assessment is bounded to the pin, native collection and inspected semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The complete-data estimator must be defined on posterior-supported completed data and have the required moments. Empty mixture components, boundary or infinite MLEs, constrained parameter spaces and nonidentifiability need explicit conventions; a conditional mean can leave a nonconvex parameter space.

Conditional expectation is the least-squares approximation to an integrable squared-error target under a fixed law. That fact does not prove decreasing true parameter error, observed-likelihood monotonicity or global convergence across ICE iterations with changing laws.

The Delmas equivalence uses the mean/expectation parameter psi, although the source calls it canonical; its natural parameter phi is distinct. The claim is not automatic for arbitrary coordinates, curved/constrained exponential families or boundary estimates. A nonlinear transformation does not generally commute with conditional expectation.

For Gaussian mixtures, expectation of a complete-data class mean or variance containing a random class count differs in general from a ratio of expected sufficient statistics. The usual Gaussian-parameter ICE update therefore cannot simply be replaced by an EM update without checking the conditions.

Monte Carlo approximation requires valid posterior sampling and appropriate convergence conditions. Correlated Gibbs samples, finite sample counts and apparently steady parameters do not by themselves certify exact expectations or convergence. A one-sample version can resemble stochastic EM for a specific complete-data estimator; it is not every stochastic-approximation EM algorithm.

The inspected examples in Delmas contain scaling/covariance notation issues, and its introductory suggestion that mixed discrete-continuous data make likelihood irrelevant is not adopted. The definition and qualified coordinate comparison do not certify all printed example formulas. Neither inspected paper provides a universal empirical performance guarantee; no fitting, benchmark or author-code run was performed.

claims.statement: Let observed data be y and hidden data h, and choose a complete-data estimator T(h,y) of a parameter theta. From a valid current theta_k, set theta_(k+1)=E_(theta_k)[T(H,y)|Y=y], when this expectation exists and remains admissible. A finite hidden space permits a posterior-weighted sum; otherwise average T over appropriate posterior samples as a Monte Carlo approximation. This average is taken after evaluating the estimator on each completed datum. It generally differs from applying a nonlinear estimator to expected sufficient statistics. With a complete-data maximum-likelihood estimator, ICE averages an argmax, whereas EM takes an argmax after averaging the log likelihood. For a regular full identifiable exponential family with a valid finite interior complete-data MLE and an invertible mean-parameter map, the expectation coordinate psi=E_theta[s(H,Y)] has complete-data estimator s(H,Y), so ICE and EM coincide in that coordinate. Nonlinear reparameterization need not preserve equality of their updates.

native_neighbors.name: Cross-entropy optimization
native_neighbors.definition: A stochastic optimization method that iteratively samples a parameterized search distribution, selects high-performing samples using an adaptive threshold, and refits the distribution by maximum likelihood on those selected samples.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This is the optimization branch of the cross-entropy method, represented by Algorithm2.3 in the inspected 2005 tutorial. It is distinct from the rare-event probability estimator, the cross-entropy loss used to train a classifier, NES natural-gradient steps, and CMA-ES evolution-path covariance adaptation. The sampling family and its fit define concrete instances; the generic algorithm is not limited to independent Bernoulli variables or a Gaussian implementation. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 285 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 15 and 15 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. limitations: A score>=threshold rule need not select exactly rho*N candidates: order-statistic indexing and tied scores can increase the elite count. Implementations must state their quantile, tie and optimization-direction conventions; minimization requires the corresponding lower-score criterion or an equivalent score transformation.

Unsmoothed finite-sample fitting can produce Bernoulli probabilities 0 or 1 and remove future exploration. Interior initialization and 0<alpha<1 prevent exact endpoints after a single convex smoothing step in exact arithmetic; smoothing alone does not guarantee exploration forever or a global optimum, and finite precision can still collapse support.

The choice of sampling family, initial support, sample size, elite fraction, fit constraints and stopping rule matters. A stabilized threshold is not an optimality certificate; the source explicitly permits getting trapped at a local minimum and limits its asymptotic discussion.

Maximum-likelihood fitting of selected candidates is a sampling-distribution update, not an unbiased gradient of raw expected fitness. It does not require derivatives of the black-box objective; solving the distribution fit may still require numerical optimization. No universal performance or convergence-rate claim is curated.

claims.statement: Specify a sampling family f(x;v), initial parameter, sample size N, elite parameter rho and stopping rule. For maximization, draw candidates from the current distribution, evaluate their scores and choose the empirical (1−rho) quantile as threshold gamma. Fit new parameters by maximizing the sum of log f(x;v) over sampled candidates with score at least gamma. The optimization formulation uses unit weights: it redefines the associated stochastic problem at each iteration, so the rare-event algorithm’s nominal-to-current likelihood ratio is absent. Optionally smooth the fitted parameter toward the old one via v_new=alpha*v_fit+(1−alpha)*v_old. For independent Bernoulli coordinates, the unsmoothed fit is the coordinatewise fraction of ones among selected samples. Iterate until the chosen stopping condition; the displayed Algorithm2.3 uses an unchanged threshold over several iterations. The source’s cross-entropy derivation minimizes KL from the ideal selected-event distribution to the parameterized sampling distribution, not the reverse direction.

native_neighbors.name: Simulated annealing
native_neighbors.definition: A stochastic optimization procedure that explores candidate configurations with temperature-controlled acceptance of cost-increasing moves and progressively cools that acceptance process to concentrate search on low-cost configurations.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes the temperature-scheduled optimization procedure exemplified by Kirkpatrick, Gelatt and Vecchi. Its basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis step is distinguished from fixed-temperature target sampling, generic annealing metaphors, training signal annealing and a proof that a particular finite schedule reaches a global minimum. The 1983 article is a primary formulation, not a claim of exclusive invention. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 285 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. Full-checkout fixed-string searches included ignored and hidden files in worktree and main, returning 15 and 15 lines respectively. Every text hit was a prior candidate lead. Nine exact AIO CLASS nodes with scoped synonyms/comments and outgoing edges and seven native neighboring mechanisms were inspected. Absence is bounded to this snapshot and semantic neighborhood.
limitations: The exp(−delta/T) expression is for positive effective temperature with the physical Boltzmann constant absorbed into its cost units. Zero temperature is a limiting or separately defined greedy rule, not evaluation of that quotient at T=0. Equal-cost moves are accepted in the displayed symmetric-proposal rule.

At fixed T the Boltzmann interpretation requires a proper target and a valid transition construction. Arbitrary asymmetric proposals do not justify dropping the reverse-to-forward proposal ratio. Lowering T changes the target; stationarity for a fixed stage does not imply equilibrium throughout a finite cooling run.

Positive-temperature uphill acceptance only permits escape through moves supported by the proposal. It does not ensure reaching every state, escaping a local basin in a chosen budget or tracking equilibrium. Rapid cooling can freeze search prematurely; schedule length, cost scale, move connectivity and constraints matter.

The primary article’s heuristics and empirical scaling claims are not a finite-run global-convergence theorem or a universal complexity bound. The later mathematical conditions for asymptotic annealing convergence were not audited here. No electronic-design or traveling-salesman benchmark is reproduced.

claims.statement: Choose a representation of feasible configurations, an objective E to minimize, a random rearrangement proposal and an annealing schedule specifying temperatures and work at each temperature. At current configuration x, propose y and compute delta=E(y)−E(x). For the basic symmetric-proposal Metropolis rule at effective temperature T>0 measured in cost units, accept delta<=0 moves and accept delta>0 with probability exp(−delta/T); otherwise retain x. Repeat transitions at the current temperature, then lower temperature according to the schedule. High temperatures permit larger cost-increasing moves more frequently; cooling reduces that probability. The source motivates sufficient equilibration at each stage. Candidate representation, move set and schedule depend on the optimization problem; the returned low-cost configuration is a search result rather than a certified global minimizer.

native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record denotes the deterministic free-energy fitting procedure described by Hofmann, with his held-out inverse-annealing schedule as an explicit realization. Ordinary EM is its beta=1 case. The procedure changes responsibilities and parameter fitting; it is neither replica-exchange MCMC nor a supervised confidence-mask schedule, and it does not introduce a new topic-model probability family. limitations: Responsibilities require a positive finite normalizer for each observed x. At positive beta, zero latent-joint entries remain zero; the beta-to-zero limit is uniform only over the positive support. beta=0 makes the displayed parameter objective independent of eta and is not included as an ordinary M-step.
This record concerns finite latent-state sums. Raising a continuous latent density to a power below one need not preserve integrability; that extension requires its own conditions.

Exact block updates concern fixed-beta free energy. They do not guarantee monotonic ordinary likelihood for beta different from one, global optimality, posterior calibration or held-out improvement. Changing beta does not optimize one unchanged objective.

The inverse-annealing schedule decreases beta after an ordinary-EM start and uses held-out decisions. It is not the same schedule as conventional deterministic-annealing cooling, and it is not a stochastic sampling transition with an invariant target. Schedule thresholds and multiplicative factors require an implementation choice.

The source’s perplexity and retrieval comparisons concern selected historical corpora and settings. No automatic prevention of overfitting, speedup, universal benefit or author-code reproduction is claimed.

claims.statement: For observations x with multiplicities n_x, finite latent states z, model parameters eta and a positive inverse temperature beta, minimize F_beta(q,eta)=sum_x n_x*sum_z q_xz*[log q_xz-beta*log p_eta(x,z)]. For fixed eta, on positive joint support use q_xz=p_eta(x,z)^beta/sum_j p_eta(x,j)^beta. For fixed q and beta>0, minimizing F_beta over eta is equivalent to maximizing the expected complete log likelihood; in PLSA this gives the usual normalized expected-count M-step with the tempered responsibilities. At beta=1 the E-step is the ordinary posterior. With 0<beta<1 it is flatter on its positive support. Hofmann’s inverse-annealing schedule first runs early-stopped EM at beta=1, then reduces beta multiplicatively, continues iterations while held-out performance improves, and stops decreasing beta when further improvements cease. At fixed beta, exact block updates optimize that temperature’s free energy; changing beta changes the objective.
